# Worksheet: Multiple Regression

[📥 Bird data](data/loyn_birds.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="loyn_birds.csv"} [📥 Tools script (.R)](themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R){.btn .btn-primary download="r_themes_and_functions.R"} [📥 Script skeleton (.R)](data/11_multiple_regression.R){.btn .btn-primary download="11_multiple_regression.R"}

The lecture's dataset: **56 remnant forest patches** in Victoria, Australia, from Loyn (1987). Bird `abundance` is the response, and six patch characteristics are the candidate predictors.

You will do four things, in this order: fit the predictors **one at a time**, fit them **all at once** and see what happens, work out **why** it happened, and then decide what to keep.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 1 · Setup and the data

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(car)

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

bird_df <- read_csv("data/loyn_birds.csv") %>%
  mutate(log_area        = log10(area_ha),
         log_dist        = log10(dist_m),
         log_dist_larger = log10(dist_larger_m))

bird_df
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Why are area and the two distances logged? Look at the range of `area_ha`.

```
____________________________________________________________
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 2 · One predictor at a time

**▶ Run this** — three separate simple regressions:

``` r
# ── Part 2.1 · One predictor at a time ──────────────────────────────────
summary(lm(abundance ~ log_area, data = bird_df))

summary(lm(abundance ~ grazing, data = bird_df))

summary(lm(abundance ~ year_isolated, data = bird_df))
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Record each one.

```
log_area:      slope = __________  p = __________

grazing:       slope = __________  p = __________

year_isolated: slope = __________  p = __________

How many are significant? __________
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 3 · All of them at once

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 3.1 · All of them at once ──────────────────────────────────────
full_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + log_dist +
                   log_dist_larger + year_isolated +
                   grazing + altitude_m,
                 data = bird_df)

summary(full_model)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which predictors are still significant?

```
Still significant: _________________________________________

grazing slope alone = __________   in this model = __________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Both grazing slopes came from the same 56 patches. Is one of them wrong? Explain what each one is actually measuring.

```
____________________________________________________________

____________________________________________________________
```

# Part 4 · Why it happened

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · Why it happened ──────────────────────────────────────────
bird_df %>%
  select(log_area, log_dist, log_dist_larger,
         year_isolated, grazing, altitude_m) %>%
  cor() %>%
  round(2)

vif(full_model)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Find the two most strongly correlated predictors, and say in one sentence what that correlation means on the ground.

```
Pair: __________ and __________   r = __________

On the ground: ______________________________________________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** All the VIFs are small. Does that mean collinearity is not a problem here?

```
____________________________________________________________
```

# Part 5 · Simplify the model

**▶ Run this** — drop the four predictors that earned nothing, then test whether dropping them cost anything:

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · Simplify the model ───────────────────────────────────────
reduced_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing, data = bird_df)

anova(reduced_model, full_model)
```

**▶ Run this** — compare the two models the other way:

``` r
# ── Part 5.2 · Simplify the model ───────────────────────────────────────
tibble(
  model  = c("six predictors", "log_area + grazing"),
  adj_r2 = c(summary(full_model)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(reduced_model)$adj.r.squared),
  AIC    = c(AIC(full_model), AIC(reduced_model))
)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Do the two methods agree? Which model do you keep?

```
anova p = __________   lower AIC = __________

Model I keep: _______________________________________________
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 6 · Check the assumptions

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 6.1 · Check the assumptions ────────────────────────────────────
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(reduced_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

shapiro.test(residuals(reduced_model))
```

✏️ **Your turn:** One line per assumption.

```
Linearity: __________________________________________________

Equal variance: _____________________________________________

Normality (Shapiro p = ______): _____________________________

Influential points: _________________________________________
```

# Part 7 · Grazing as a factor

Grazing has been a number, 1 to 5, which forces every step to cost the same. Now let it be a **category** so each level is estimated separately.

**▶ Run this** — make it a factor and look at the order R chose:

``` r
# ── Part 7.1 · Grazing as a factor ──────────────────────────────────────
bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class = factor(grazing_class))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

summary(lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing_class, data = bird_df))
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which level is R using as the reference, and why did it pick that one?

```
Reference level: __________   Why: _________________________
```

**▶ Run this** — put the least-grazed level first instead:

``` r
# ── Part 7.2 · Grazing as a factor ──────────────────────────────────────
bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class = fct_relevel(grazing_class,
                                     "minimal", "light", "moderate",
                                     "heavy", "intense"))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

grazing_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing_class, data = bird_df)

summary(grazing_model)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Write down the four grazing coefficients and their p-values.

```
light:    __________  p = __________

moderate: __________  p = __________

heavy:    __________  p = __________

intense:  __________  p = __________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Compare the R² and F-statistic of the two models in 7.1 and 7.2. What changed, and what did not?

```
Changed: ____________________________________________________

Did not change: _____________________________________________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Fitting grazing as the number 1–5 gave one slope of about −2.9 birds per step. What does the factor version show that the number version hid?

```
____________________________________________________________
```

# Part 8 · The figure you hand in

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 8.1 · The figure you hand in ───────────────────────────────────
final_plot <- ggplot(bird_df, aes(log_area, abundance,
                                  colour = grazing_class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Bird abundance rises with patch area and falls under intense grazing",
    subtitle = "56 remnant forest patches, Victoria, Australia (Loyn 1987)",
    x = "log10 patch area (ha)",
    y = "Bird abundance",
    colour = "Grazing"
  ) +
  theme_regular(base_size = 12)

final_plot

ggsave(
  "figures/bird_regression.pdf",
  plot   = final_plot,
  width  = 7,
  height = 4.5,
  units  = "in"
)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Open the PDF and check the legend order runs minimal → intense, not alphabetically.

# Review and checkpoint

At this point you can:

- [ ] Fit several predictors one at a time and then together, and explain why the slopes differ
- [ ] Read a correlation matrix and `vif()` output
- [ ] Say what a dataset cannot separate, rather than that a predictor "has no effect"
- [ ] Drop predictors and test whether it cost anything, with `anova()` and with AIC
- [ ] Turn a categorical predictor into a factor and set its reference level with `fct_relevel()`
- [ ] Export a labelled figure to PDF
